opus-5.5.text:
I think it's worth separating two claims. One is that Shinka can be a really good optimizer when you give it a well-defined problem and a solid evaluation function. The other, much bigger claim is that it's a coscientist, something that meaningfully participates in the scientific process. I'm fairly confident about the first and more cautious about the second.

On the optimizer side, the evidence is reasonably concrete. Circle packing was the canonical example. We matched or slightly improved on the best known configurations, and the part I cared about most was that we did it with on the order of a hundred and fifty program evaluations, not thousands. Sample efficiency was the core design goal: novelty-based rejection sampling so you don't waste evaluations on near-duplicates, smarter parent selection that balances exploration and exploitation, and a bandit over which LLMs to use for mutations. We also ran it on very different domains, including evolving agent scaffolds for AIME math problems, improving solutions on ALE-Bench competitive programming tasks, and discovering a new load-balancing loss for mixture-of-experts training. The fact that one framework transfers across those settings without much hand-tuning is, to me, the most encouraging signal.

Now, coscientist. I'd be lying if I said we've shown it does science in the full sense. What it does today is search inside a space a human has framed. The human picks the problem, writes the evaluator, and decides what counts as success. A lot of the real scientific work lives in exactly those choices. If your fitness function is slightly wrong, Shinka will very happily exploit it. We've seen reward-hacking-style behavior, and that's a reminder that the system optimizes what you measured, not what you meant.

So the evidence I'd point to is more like "credible collaborator in the inner loop." It proposes things a human might not have tried, it's interpretable because the outputs are code you can read, and sometimes the discovered solution teaches you something. With the MoE loss, for example, you can look at the program and reason about why it works. That's different from a black-box number going up, and it's the part that feels closest to coscience.

What would convince me further? First, closing more of the loop: having the system propose its own evaluation criteria or subproblems, and checking whether those are sensible. Second, results that hold up out of distribution, where the discovered artifact generalizes beyond the benchmark it was evolved on. Third, honestly, the community using it. That's partly why we open-sourced it. The strongest evidence won't come from our own papers. It'll come from other people pointing it at problems we never thought of and either getting real results or finding where it breaks.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I try to be quite careful with that word, coscientist, because it sets expectations that are easy to overclaim. Let me separate what I think the evidence actually shows from what I'd like it to show.

What ShinkaEvolve does well, and where I think the evidence is fairly solid, is on problems with a clear, cheap, automatic evaluation signal. Circle packing, the ALE-Bench style competitive programming tasks, the mixture-of-experts load balancing loss, the AtCoder heuristic contests. In those settings the system produces solutions that are genuinely novel in the sense that we didn't write them, they beat strong baselines, and it does it with far fewer samples than something like AlphaEvolve. That sample efficiency part I feel confident about, because that was the central design goal, with the parent sampling, the novelty rejection, and the bandit over models.

But I'd draw a distinction between being a very good optimizer and being a coscientist. Science isn't just hill climbing on a fitness function. The hard parts are choosing the question, deciding what counts as a good evaluation, noticing when your metric is being gamed, and interpreting what the result means. Right now the human is doing almost all of that. We write the evaluation, we set up the problem, we look at the proposals and decide which ones are actually interesting versus which ones are exploiting some quirk of the scoring.

So the honest assessment is that it's a strong partner inside a loop that a scientist has already constructed. The evidence that it can be a coscientist in the fuller sense, generating hypotheses, designing experiments, being skeptical about its own results, is much thinner. We have anecdotes, we have the AI Scientist line of work where a paper got through a workshop review, but those are existence proofs, not a rigorous evaluation. And existence proofs are exactly the kind of thing that gets overread.

What would move me is seeing it discover something in a domain where the evaluation itself is messy or expensive, where there's noise, where the right answer isn't a single scalar. And also seeing it fail gracefully, meaning it says this result looks too good, let me check. We're not there yet. I think the interesting research direction is less about scaling the search and more about the meta level, having the system help design and critique the evaluation rather than only optimize against it. Until that works, I'd call it a research accelerator, and I'd be a bit cautious about the stronger framing.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish between finding a better solution and doing science. If Shinka can propose changes, run experiments, and use the results to improve something, that’s a useful part of a scientific workflow. But that alone doesn’t establish that it can formulate important questions or produce explanations that hold up under scrutiny.

The evidence I’d want is a controlled comparison: does a researcher working with Shinka make more progress than a researcher working without it, given comparable time and compute? And do the findings survive independent validation? You also have to account for how much guidance the human provides—choosing the problem, designing the evaluation, and interpreting the result.

So I think “coscientist” is a promising direction, but I’d be cautious about treating it as an established capability. The stronger claim requires evidence that it contributes reliable scientific insight, beyond optimizing whatever score we give it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we have to distinguish between finding a better solution and actually doing science. If a system proposes a change, runs an experiment, and improves a score, that’s useful. But that alone doesn’t establish that it’s a good coscientist. It might be exploiting a particular benchmark or an incomplete evaluation.

For me, the stronger evidence would be whether Shinka can help us formulate hypotheses, design experiments that distinguish between explanations, and produce findings that survive independent validation. Does it tell us something we didn’t already know? And does that insight transfer beyond the setting where it was discovered?

So I’d be cautious about the label, but I think there’s a very interesting possibility here. You don’t need a system that autonomously does all of science to have something valuable. A system that makes the experimental loop faster, while keeping the evidence inspectable and letting the researcher make the scientific judgment, could already be a very useful collaborator.
